newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Further strains in Israel-PLO relations.
newsitem.headline: Further strains in Israel-PLO relations.

text.p: An Arab guerrilla attack that killed a Jewish settler mother and her child and Israeli plans to build homes for Jews in an Arab Jerusalem area have further strained PLO-Israel relations.

Israeli Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechai said George Habash's Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine (PFLP) was responsible for the drive-by killing of the two Israelis in the West Bank on Wednesday. The woman's husband and four other children were wounded in the attack.
The PFLP opposes the interim PLO-Israel peace deals.
The Israeli army announced it had sealed off the PLO-ruled Ramallah enclave in the West Bank to which it said the attackers fled.

President Yasser Arafat's Palestinian Authority could do more to curb guerrillas and if it had "perhaps it would have been possible to prevent this attack", Mordechai told a news conference broadcast live by Israeli radio and television.
Israeli Finance Minister Dan Meridor told Israel's Itim news agency: "It is not possible to continue to conduct peace negotiations accompanied by incidents of this sort".

But Mordechai, asked how talks with the Palestinians on issues such as the long-delayed Israeli troop pullout from the West Bank town of Hebron would be affected by the attack, said now was not the time to decide.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said the drive-by killings and the apparent fleeing of the gunmen to Ramallah posed a "test" for Arafat.

"We expect that they will extradite and first of all help us to arrest these murderers of children, murders of women...We will not let up until we catch them," Netanyahu told reporters at a Jerusalem hospital after visiting the wounded.
"Whoever thinks that the Jewish people can be uprooted from its land, from the heart of the Jewish homeland by these acts of terror should know that we will uproot him," said Netanyahu.
He said he would consult cabinet ministers on Thursday on what steps Israel should take in the wake of the attack.

Security cooperation enshrined in the interim peace deals signed by the Palestine Liberation Organisation (PLO) and Israel's previous centre-left government worked on Wednesday. Israeli troops did not invade Ramallah despite Jewish settler demands that they should do so.

Mordechai said the attackers fled in the direction of Ramallah and that their abandoned, torched car was discovered there. Israeli troops entered the self-rule enclave in coordination with Palestinian forces to investigate.

PLO officials, enraged at initially approved Israeli plans to build housing units in the heart of a Palestinian neighbourhood in Arab East Jerusalem, condemned the attack but said they thought Israel would exploit it to circumvent peace moves.
"The Palestinian Authority condemns this suspicious act...(it) considers this act directed at this specific time against the Palestinian Authority," a PLO official told Reuters.
"It serves the Israeli side's attempts to escape from carrying out the commitments which have been agreed upon and it helps to cover its playing with the peace process."

The Jerusalem District Planning Commission's decision to approve the construction plans was condemned by Arafat as a violation of peace deals. Jerusalem's future is to be negotiated in final peace talks which have yet to resume since the right-wing Netanyahu took office in June.
Israel's opening of an entrance to a tunnel close to Moslem holy sites in Jerusalem in September ignited a wave of violence that killed 60 Palestinians and 15 Israelis.
Palestinians have warned that if the construction plan is signed by an Israeli minister, the last approval it needs, it could spur violence much worse than that in September.
